content: Epidemiological studies have suggested a potential association between the use of beta2-agonists and an increase in asthma-related mortality. This has led to ongoing debate regarding the safety of long-term use of long-acting beta2-agonists (LABAs) when combined with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS). This updated Cochrane Review incorporates data from two large trials, which included 23,422 adolescents and adults, conducted as part of a mandate by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The objective of this review was to evaluate the risk of mortality and non-fatal serious adverse events (SAEs) in individuals with chronic asthma who were randomly assigned to receive regular formoterol combined with ICS versus ICS alone. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register, clinical trial registries, and FDA submissions. The most recent search was conducted in February 2019. Eligible studies included RCTs with a parallel design involving adults, children, or both, with asthma of any severity, who received treatment for at least 12 weeks. A total of 42 studies met the inclusion criteria, with 39 studies included in the analysis. These studies involved 35,751 adults and 4,035 children and adolescents. The ICS used in the studies included beclomethasone (200–800 µg daily), budesonide (200–1600 µg daily), fluticasone (200–250 µg daily), and mometasone (200–800 µg daily). Formoterol doses ranged from 12 to 48 µg daily. Most studies used fixed-dose combination ICS. The risk of selection bias, performance bias, and attrition bias was judged to be low, but most studies did not independently assess the causation of SAEs. Mortality: Among adults, 17 of 18,645 participants receiving formoterol and ICS and 13 of 17,106 participants receiving ICS alone died from any cause. The pooled Peto odds ratio (OR) was 1.25 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61 to 2.56), representing moderate-certainty evidence. This equates to approximately one death per 1,000 adults treated with either ICS alone or formoterol and ICS over 26 weeks (95% CI 0 to 2 deaths). No deaths were reported in children and adolescents (4,035 participants), but the certainty of this evidence was low. Regarding asthma-related deaths, no children or adolescents died from asthma. However, three of 12,777 adults in the formoterol and ICS group died from asthma-related causes. This evidence was of low certainty. Non-Fatal Serious Adverse Events (SAEs): Among adults, 401 participants experienced a non-fatal SAE of any cause while on formoterol and ICS, compared to 369 participants on ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.00 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.16), representing high-certainty evidence. For every 1,000 adults treated with ICS alone for 26 weeks, 22 experienced an SAE, and the same risk was observed for those on formoterol and ICS (95% CI 19 to 25). Among children and adolescents, 30 of 2,491 participants on formoterol and ICS experienced an SAE, compared to 13 of 1,544 participants on ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.33 (95% CI 0.71 to 2.49), representing moderate-certainty evidence. For every 1,000 children and adolescents treated with ICS alone for 12.5 weeks, 8 experienced an SAE, compared to 11 on formoterol and ICS (95% CI 6 to 21). Asthma-Related Serious Adverse Events: Among adults, 90 participants experienced an asthma-related non-fatal SAE while on formoterol and ICS, compared to 102 participants on ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 0.86 (95% CI 0.64 to 1.14), representing moderate-certainty evidence. For every 1,000 adults treated with ICS alone for 26 weeks, 6 experienced an asthma-related SAE, compared to 5 on formoterol and ICS (95% CI 4 to 7). Among children and adolescents, 9 participants experienced an asthma-related non-fatal SAE while on formoterol and ICS, compared to 5 participants on ICS alone. The pooled Peto OR was 1.18 (95% CI 0.40 to 3.51), representing very low-certainty evidence. For every 1,000 children and adolescents treated with ICS alone for 12.5 weeks, 3 experienced an asthma-related SAE, compared to 4 on formoterol and ICS (95% CI 1 to 11). Authors' Conclusions: The review did not find a significant difference in the risk of all-cause or asthma-related mortality in adults treated with formoterol and ICS compared to ICS alone. The certainty of this evidence ranged from moderate to low. No deaths were reported in children and adolescents, but the evidence remains uncertain in this age group. The overall risk of death was very low for both treatment groups, but the possibility of a difference in mortality risk with the addition of formoterol to ICS cannot be ruled out. There was no difference in the risk of non-fatal SAEs of any cause in adults (high-certainty evidence). While a previous version of this review suggested a lower risk of asthma-related SAEs in adults treated with formoterol and ICS, the inclusion of new studies has eliminated this observed difference (moderate-certainty evidence). The number of children and adolescents with SAEs was small, leading to continued uncertainty in this population. Clinical decisions regarding the regular use of formoterol and ICS should carefully weigh the known symptomatic benefits of this combination therapy against the remaining uncertainties about its potential risks.
